demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Triggers.value: Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad
I force myself to think only positive thoughts
I try to push them out of my mind

Threat.value: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel

Memory.value: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once

Negative Appraisals.value: There is something wrong with me as a person
I have to be on guard all the time
The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: Contamination appraisals are hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma of accidentally causing serious injury to another person; for this trauma type, guilt, responsibility, danger, or moral failure would be more coherent than feeling physically dirty/contaminated, absent any assault or bodily violation context.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Other-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what other people have done to me
issues.explanation: Other-blame rumination conflicts with the trauma type and the rest of the profile: the central event is that he accidentally injured another person, while the appraisals emphasize defectiveness and threat rather than victimization by others. Dwelling on what other people have done to me points to a different trauma narrative.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Magical Thinking: I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad
issues.explanation: Magical thinking that the event did not really happen or was not that bad sits awkwardly with the very high-severity profile and with simultaneous endorsement of full sensory reliving plus strong persistent threat and self-defectiveness. Partial minimization can occur, but this item as phrased is in notable tension with the rest of the profile.

vignette:
Rajesh stood at the window of his small apartment, watching the rain fall on the parking lot below. He was eighty years old, a widower for six years now, and a retired Coast Guard veteran who had spent the better part of his life on the water. He had joined the service at nineteen, fresh off a boat from Mumbai, and had risen through the ranks with a steady hand and a quiet sense of duty. But that duty had broken him one gray afternoon off the coast of Alaska, when a routine rescue operation had gone catastrophically wrong.

It had been a storm, the kind that turned the sea into a churning wall of white and black. A fishing vessel had sent a distress call, and Rajesh had been second-in-command on the cutter that responded. The seas were too high for a direct approach, so they launched a smaller inflatable boat to pull the fishermen off the deck. Rajesh was operating the winch, lowering the basket down through the spray. He saw a young man, maybe twenty-five, waving from the rail. The boat lurched. The cable snapped. The basket swung hard and struck the man across the skull, sending him into the water. They recovered his body twenty minutes later, but he was already gone. Rajesh had killed a man with his own hands, even if those hands had only been operating a machine. The Coast Guard ruled it an accident. Rajesh never believed them.

What he remembered now, at eighty, came in pieces that did not fit together. He could see the young man’s face, but only in flashes—the open mouth, the wet hair, the eyes that looked surprised. He could hear the sound of the cable snapping, a sharp metallic crack, but he could not place it in sequence. He could feel the cold spray on his cheek, the vibration of the winch through his gloves, the sickening jolt when the basket hit. But when he tried to deliberately recall the moment—when his therapist had asked him, years later, to walk through it—the memory would dissolve into static, leaving only a hollow dread in his chest. At other times, the memory would return on its own, unbidden, and it would feel completely real: the salt in his nostrils, the scream of the wind, the weight of the cable in his hands, the sight of the basket swinging. He would be back on that deck, and he would be forty years younger, and he would be killing a man again.

After the accident, Rajesh had told himself it did not really happen. He had spent weeks replaying the event in his head, then forcing himself to stop. He would think of the weather report, the maintenance logs, the paperwork—anything to keep the image from forming fully. He had learned to force himself to think only positive thoughts: the lives he had saved, the years of service, the medals. But underneath the reframing, a deeper belief had taken root: there was something wrong with him as a person. The event had happened to him because of the sort of man he was. He had been careless, or arrogant, or cursed. He had been the kind of man who killed people, even when he was trying to save them.

That belief followed him into retirement. He had stopped going to unfamiliar places because he could not assess the danger. He could not walk into a new store or a park he had never visited without feeling a creeping sense that something terrible was about to happen, that he would cause it again. He had begun to take too many risks in other parts of his life—driving too fast, walking through bad neighborhoods at night—as if daring the universe to punish him properly. And he always chose where to sit based on how safe he felt: back to the wall, exit visible, nothing behind him. His daughter had noticed. She would ask why he always sat in the same corner of the restaurant, and he would say it was the light.

The world had become a place of constant threat. He had to be on guard all the time. A siren in the distance—an ambulance, a police car—would freeze him mid-step, his heart hammering, his hands tingling, because the sound was the same pitch as the cutter’s warning horn that day. Being in nature, especially near any body of water, would trigger a flood of sensory fragments: the salt, the cold, the lurch of the deck. He could not walk along the river near his apartment without feeling the floor drop out from under him. And when his daughter talked about the future—her plans to retire, her son’s college applications—Rajesh would feel a cold dread settle in his stomach. The future was a place where he did not belong. The future was where he would have to live with what he had done.

He had come to the clinic because his daughter had finally insisted. She had found him one evening, sitting in the dark, staring at the wall. He had not told her what he was thinking. What frightened him most was not the memory itself, but the certainty that he could never be forgiven—not by the dead man, not by his family, not by himself. He was hoping, though he could not say it out loud, that someone might tell him he was wrong.
